identity.title: Soil Moisture Monitor
identity.tagline: A plant that tells you when it's thirsty, via an LED instead of wilting.

goal: Stick a probe into a plant's soil and light an LED the moment it dries out past a comfortable threshold — a genuinely useful little gadget, and a straightforward second example (after the Light-Activated Night Lamp) of reading an analog sensor and reacting to a threshold.
simpleSummary: Stick a probe in a plant's soil and light an LED when it needs water.
howItWorks: The two exposed probes on a soil moisture sensor form a simple resistance measurement: dry soil conducts electricity poorly, wet soil conducts it much better. The sensor's onboard circuit converts that resistance into an analog voltage on its AOUT pin, which analogRead() reads as a number from 0 to 1023. Unlike the rain sensor's simplified digital output, this project reads that raw analog value directly, which means the code — not a fixed onboard comparator — decides exactly what "too dry" means, and can be tuned freely for a specific plant or soil type.
toolsNeeded: Arduino IDE (free, installed on your computer)
USB cable to connect the board to your computer
A potted plant (or a cup of soil) to test the probe in
circuitDiagramCaption: Sensor's analog output (AOUT) on A0; "needs water" LED on D9.

wiringSteps.instruction: Wire the sensor's VCC to Arduino 5V, GND to GND, and AOUT to A0.
wiringSteps.detail: This project deliberately uses AOUT (the raw analog reading) rather than DOUT, so the code can define its own moisture threshold instead of relying on the sensor board's onboard potentiometer.

wiringSteps.instruction: Wire the LED and its 220Ω resistor between D9 and GND, same as LED Blink.
wiringSteps.detail: Nothing new here — this is the same LED circuit used throughout the beginner projects.

wiringSteps.instruction: Insert only the two metal probes into the soil, keeping the sensor's small circuit board above the surface and dry.
wiringSteps.detail: The bare probes corrode over time when constantly powered in wet soil — see Troubleshooting for a simple fix if you're leaving this running long-term.

code.explanation: Same threshold pattern as the Light-Activated Night Lamp project: read a raw analog value, print it while tuning, and compare it against a constant that represents "time to act." On most of these resistive sensors, a higher reading means less conductivity, which means drier soil — but confirm this against your own sensor's actual behavior in the Serial Monitor rather than assuming, since some sensor variants report the opposite direction.

expectedBehavior: The LED stays off in moist soil and turns on once the sensor dries out past the DRY_THRESHOLD value, which you tune to match your specific plant's soil and the sensor's real-world range.

troubleshooting.issue: Reading never changes no matter how wet or dry the soil is.
troubleshooting.fix: Confirm both probes are actually inserted into the soil (not just one), and that AOUT — not DOUT — is wired to A0.

troubleshooting.issue: LED logic seems backwards (on when wet, off when dry).
troubleshooting.fix: Flip the comparison operator, or confirm your specific sensor board's polarity by watching raw Serial values while manually wetting and drying the probes.

troubleshooting.issue: Sensor corrodes or reads increasingly inaccurately after days of continuous use.
troubleshooting.fix: This is a well-known issue with resistive soil sensors left constantly powered — power the sensor from a digital pin instead of a permanent 5V connection, and only turn it on for the brief moment it takes a reading.

extensions: Power the sensor intermittently from a digital output pin instead of a constant 5V rail to reduce probe corrosion over time.
Add a small water pump (via a relay) that runs automatically when soil is too dry.
Display the live moisture percentage on an LCD instead of a simple LED threshold.
Combine with the Rain Alarm project so outdoor plants skip a scheduled watering if it's already rained.
